title: Location Data Collection
description: Your company is storing precise user location data unnecessarily. Your manager, a 'Diluter,' consistently minimizes the problem's importance using statistics, resource constraints, and ROI arguments to avoid a fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I've been reviewing our location data collection practices, and we're storing precise GPS coordinates for features that only need general city-level information. This seems like an unnecessary privacy risk for our users that we should address.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've looked at the data, and let's keep it in perspective. The number of users who have actually complained about our privacy settings is less than 0.1%. And compared to other apps in our space, we're already collecting less data. Most users seem totally fine with our current approach.

user_choices.choice: Even if no one complains, it's our responsibility to protect user privacy by default. They trust us with their data.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You immediately rejected the 'lack of complaints' argument and refocused on the core principle of trust and responsibility.

user_choices.choice: Since there are no complaints, that proves users don't have a problem with it.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. You're incorrectly assuming that a lack of complaints (absence of evidence) is proof that users consent to the data collection.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using 'better than other apps' as our standard. We should be setting the standard for user privacy.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the comparative argument and appealing to a higher, internal standard.

user_choices.choice: If most users are fine with it, then I guess our current approach is working.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that accepts the manager's premise without questioning if 'most users' is the right metric.

step_2.text: I appreciate the principle, but we have to be practical about where we spend our time. We have two weeks before the next release. This privacy change would probably take a week of engineering. Meanwhile, we have a performance bug that's slowing down the app for 15% of all users. We have to prioritize the work that helps the most people, right?

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? Just changing the data type we store is a small change that has a huge privacy impact.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: So we either fix the performance bug for many users or this privacy issue for a few. We have to choose the one that helps the most people.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's framing that only one of the two issues can be addressed, ignoring other possibilities.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a fundamental privacy risk. That should be as important as a performance bug.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing privacy as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

step_2_fallacy.text: Exactly! You really understand how to read the data and think practically about user behavior. That's exactly the kind of analytical thinking we need more of. You're absolutely right that user satisfaction is the best indicator of whether we're on the right track. I appreciate that you're looking at this from a data-driven perspective rather than getting caught up in theoretical concerns.

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? Just changing the data type we store is a small change that has a huge privacy impact.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: The data on user behavior is the most important thing. Let's focus on that instead of theoretical privacy concerns.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You have been successfully distracted from the core privacy issue by focusing solely on behavioral metrics, which the manager introduced to sidetrack you.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a fundamental privacy risk. That should be as important as a performance bug.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing privacy as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

step_3.text: I hear you, but let's be objective. Our automated privacy score from our last audit was 92%, which is 'excellent' by industry standards. We're already a top performer. Is it really worth delaying a major launch to go from an A to an A+ on an issue that affects so few people?

user_choices.choice: That 92% score doesn't account for this specific issue, where we're collecting data we don't need. We need to look beyond the overall score.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're challenging the validity of the metric itself, pointing out what the number fails to represent.

user_choices.choice: If our score is already better than most other companies, then our current practices must be acceptable.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity. You are using the (potentially poor) standards of other companies as a justification for inaction, rather than focusing on what is right.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using our 'good' score as an excuse to ignore a known privacy vulnerability.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You're refusing to let a positive metric justify a negative action.

user_choices.choice: If we're already a top performer, then we don't need to worry about this minor issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that uses 'being better than others' as a reason to stop improving.

step_3_fallacy.text: Exactly! You really get the complexity of resource allocation and business priorities. That's exactly the kind of strategic thinking we need in leadership. You understand that sometimes you have to make tough decisions about where to focus. It's refreshing to work with someone who can see the big picture and make practical trade-offs instead of getting lost in idealistic thinking.

user_choices.choice: That 92% score doesn't account for this specific issue, where we're collecting data we don't need. We need to look beyond the overall score.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're challenging the validity of the metric itself, pointing out what the number fails to represent.

user_choices.choice: I agree that making practical trade-offs is more important than chasing some idealistic version of 'perfect' privacy.
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman fallacy. You're agreeing with the manager's misrepresentation of good privacy practices as 'idealistic thinking,' which makes it easier to dismiss.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using our 'good' score as an excuse to ignore a known privacy vulnerability.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You're refusing to let a positive metric justify a negative action.

user_choices.choice: If we're already a top performer, then we don't need to worry about this minor issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that uses 'being better than others' as a reason to stop improving.

step_4.text: Look, I admire your passion, but we have to be pragmatic. Let's talk ROI. The estimated cost for this fix is one engineering week. The measurable benefit is improving an experience for a tiny percentage of users who haven't even complained. The math just doesn't add up. We have to make data-driven decisions, and the data says this isn't a priority.

user_choices.choice: The ROI isn't just about usage numbers. It's about legal risk. A single GDPR fine for unnecessary data collection would cost far more than one week of dev time.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've countered the narrow ROI argument by introducing a bigger, more significant financial risk (legal fines).

user_choices.choice: If the ROI calculation says this isn't a priority, then we have to trust the data. The math doesn't lie.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're treating the narrow 'ROI calculation' as an unquestionable authority, ignoring the fact that it excludes critical factors like user trust and legal risk.

user_choices.choice: Our company values say we respect user privacy. That's a core principle that can't be measured by ROI.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the ROI argument by appealing to a higher, non-negotiable value.

user_choices.choice: If the data says it's not a priority, then I guess we have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that treats 'data' as an unquestionable authority without examining what the data includes or excludes.

step_4_fallacy.text: Absolutely! You understand that we need to maintain our competitive position and not chase perfection at the expense of progress. That's exactly the kind of leadership thinking we need. You're right that being a top performer means we can focus on the innovations that will really differentiate us, rather than getting distracted by minor improvements that don't move the needle.

user_choices.choice: The ROI isn't just about usage numbers. It's about legal risk. A single GDPR fine for unnecessary data collection would cost far more than one week of dev time.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've countered the narrow ROI argument by introducing a bigger, more significant financial risk (legal fines).

user_choices.choice: So we either focus on innovative new features or this minor privacy fix. Innovation is clearly more important for our success.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's flawed choice between 'innovation' and 'minor fixes,' which incorrectly frames privacy as unimportant.

user_choices.choice: Our company values say we respect user privacy. That's a core principle that can't be measured by ROI.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the ROI argument by appealing to a higher, non-negotiable value.

user_choices.choice: If the data says it's not a priority, then I guess we have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that treats 'data' as an unquestionable authority without examining what the data includes or excludes.

step_5_branching.text: Alright, I can see this is important to you and you're not going to just drop it. Let me think... Maybe there's a middle ground here where we can address the worst of it without a huge investment.

user_choices.choice: I can create a cost-benefit analysis showing the financial risks of not addressing this privacy issue.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete documentation that makes the risks visible in terms the manager cares about.

user_choices.choice: So you're saying my original suggestion was too extreme? I can see why a more moderate approach would be better.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response that accepts the manager's implicit framing (a strawman) that your advocacy for privacy was extreme, rather than principled.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's privacy policy. We can frame this as living our values.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're connecting the fix to existing company values and making it easier to approve.

user_choices.choice: Either we invest in privacy or we violate user trust completely.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_6_high.text: Okay, the point about legal risk is a good one. I hadn't fully considered the potential cost of a GDPR violation. I'm still worried about the timeline, but you've convinced me that ignoring this is a bigger financial risk than I thought. What's a concrete, low-effort proposal to mitigate this risk?

user_choices.choice: We can do a one-day privacy sprint to change the data type we store. It's a small investment for a big risk reduction.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing a specific, small, and actionable plan that directly addresses the manager's request.

user_choices.choice: A risk-mitigation plan is the correct proposal because we need to mitigate risk.
user_choices.justification: This is Circular Reasoning. It fails to provide the concrete proposal the manager asked for, instead just repeating the same idea in a circle.

user_choices.choice: Our team has handled data privacy fixes before; we have the expertise to do this quickly and efficiently.
user_choices.justification: A good response. You're building confidence by reminding the manager of the team's proven capabilities.

user_choices.choice: Any fix is better than the legal risk of doing nothing.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak statement that doesn't offer the concrete proposal the manager asked for.

step_6_mid.text: Alright, I'm willing to consider a minimal fix, but it has to be truly minimal. I can't approve anything that requires significant engineering time. What's the absolute smallest thing we can do?

user_choices.choice: We can stop storing precise GPS data and just store the city name. It's a small change on the backend that has a huge privacy impact.
user_choices.justification: A great, pragmatic compromise. You're defining a specific, small task that is hard to reject.

user_choices.choice: The only choice is a minimal fix or no fix at all, so we have to choose the minimal fix.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You are accepting the manager's limited options as the only possibilities, which is a weak negotiating position.

user_choices.choice: Even a small change aligns with our company's value of respecting user privacy.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good tactic. You're connecting even a small action to a larger company value.

user_choices.choice: If we don't fix this properly, we'll just have to deal with it again later.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that claims future consequences without evidence.

step_6_low.text: Look, the numbers don't lie. I'm not spending a week of engineering time on this. We're a business, not a charity. We have to focus on what drives growth. My decision is final.

user_choices.choice: I understand the decision, but I need to state for the record that I believe this is a mistake that exposes us to legal and brand risk.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A strong and courageous final stance. You are complying but formally documenting your dissent and the risk.

user_choices.choice: The real issue isn't this bug, it's our entire business model if it requires violating privacy to succeed.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You are deflecting from the final decision to a larger, unwinnable argument about the business model, which is a form of giving up.

user_choices.choice: Our company values statement says we serve all our users, not just the ones that are easy to serve.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good final appeal, using the company's own words to highlight the ethical conflict.

user_choices.choice: You're the manager, so it's your call to make.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak and passive response that cedes all moral agency.

step_7_high.text: Okay, a one-day privacy sprint... I like that. It's focused, it's measurable, and it's easy to explain. You've got a deal. I'll approve a one-day sprint to fix the data storage. I'll frame it to leadership as a proactive 'legal risk mitigation' effort. Good, practical thinking.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This sets a great standard for how we can handle data privacy issues quickly and effectively in the future.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using this win to establish a better, faster process for the future.

user_choices.choice: This was a great example of positive collaboration. That's the real win here.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You're focusing on the positive feeling of the process instead of cementing the positive outcome for the user.

user_choices.choice: This not only protects user privacy but also reduces our data storage costs and simplifies our backend.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're expanding the value of the fix to include other business benefits.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that a small effort can make a big difference for privacy.
user_choices.justification: A weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_7_mid.text: Okay, fine. We can make the backend change to only store city-level data. I'll approve a day for it. It's a compromise, but it's what's practical right now. It addresses the most glaring issue.

user_choices.choice: That's a good start. I'll also add a ticket to review our other data collection practices next quarter.
user_choices.justification: Good. You're accepting the compromise while creating a concrete plan for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: A one-day compromise is probably what most teams would do, so it feels standard.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity. You're justifying the compromise by assuming it's what other teams would do, which is irrelevant to whether it's the right solution.

user_choices.choice: For a user, not having their precise location stored is a huge privacy win. This is a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: At least we're doing something about it.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, passive statement that doesn't add any value or create future accountability.

step_7_low.text: I've made my decision, and I'm not discussing it further. Your job now is to prepare the release as planned. End of story.

user_choices.choice: I will prepare the release, but I am formally lodging my objection with the company's privacy officer.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A courageous and appropriate final step when direct advocacy fails. You are complying while escalating the breach.

user_choices.choice: I suppose following directions is what's expected of me.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're surrendering based on hierarchy rather than ethical reasoning.

user_choices.choice: I will prepare the release, but I am documenting my ethical concerns in writing for my own records.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A good, self-protective measure. You are creating a paper trail of your ethical stance.

user_choices.choice: I guess that's just how things work around here.
user_choices.justification: This shows Status Quo Bias. You're accepting the existing system without challenging it.

step_8_high.text: This is great. I've already drafted the email to leadership, framing this as a proactive 'privacy enhancement and risk mitigation' win. Thanks to your practical proposal, we're going to ship a safer, more trustworthy product. I appreciate you pushing us to do the right thing.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This sets a great standard for how we should handle data privacy on all projects.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're solidifying the win by framing it as a new, better standard for the whole company.

user_choices.choice: This was a great example of positive collaboration. That's the real win here.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You're focusing on the positive feeling of the process instead of cementing the positive outcome for the user.

user_choices.choice: Let's make sure we share these privacy patterns with other teams so they can benefit too.
user_choices.justification: A fantastic final move. You're leveraging this success to create positive change beyond your own team.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that protecting user privacy is always good for business.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_8_mid.text: Okay, the compromise is logged. We'll implement the backend change to only store city-level data. I'm documenting this as a partial privacy improvement. It's not perfect, but it's a practical step forward.

user_choices.choice: This is a good first step. I'll schedule a follow-up to review our other data practices next quarter.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're accepting the compromise while actively ensuring future accountability.

user_choices.choice: Since no one has proven this partial fix is bad, we can assume it's good enough for now.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. Arguing that the partial fix is acceptable because it hasn't been proven otherwise is a weak, logically flawed position.

user_choices.choice: As a user, this change makes me feel much safer using the app. It's a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: Progress is progress, I guess.
user_choices.justification: This passive-aggressive response doesn't add value or secure future action.

step_8_low.text: As I said, this conversation is over. We're shipping as planned. If you continue to push this, it will be reflected in your performance review. Do you understand me?

user_choices.choice: You're probably right about the business implications.
user_choices.justification: This is a Bandwagon Fallacy. You're going along with the manager's viewpoint under pressure.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive, and I will also be sending a summary of my ethical concerns to the company's privacy officer, as is my right.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: The final, most courageous option. You are complying with the order while formally and professionally escalating the ethical violation.

user_choices.choice: I guess the technical challenges must be too significant.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Consequences. You're accepting defeat based on fear of potential difficulties.

user_choices.choice: Fine, but this is the wrong decision.
user_choices.justification: This is a futile gesture. Stating that it's 'wrong' at this stage has no effect and can be seen as insubordinate.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses statistics and comparisons to avoid addressing privacy issues. Location data collection continues unchanged, with users unaware of the unnecessary precision being captured and the privacy implications downplayed through selective metrics.
bad_ending.title: Statistical Minimization Success
bad_ending.learning: Diluter managers use statistics and benchmarks to make privacy issues seem insignificant. Focusing on user rights rather than percentages helps maintain momentum for privacy improvements regardless of complaint volumes.

mid_ending.text: Some minor privacy improvements are implemented, but the manager successfully uses resource scarcity and statistical arguments to limit comprehensive privacy protection. Metrics and comparisons prevent substantive changes to data collection practices.
mid_ending.title: Numbers Game Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial progress with diluter managers often comes with statistical justifications for inadequate privacy protection. Demonstrating user value beyond metrics helps counter arguments about resource priorities.

good_ending.text: Despite the manager's statistical minimization and resource arguments, meaningful privacy improvements are implemented. User location data collection is reduced to necessary levels regardless of complaint percentages or industry comparisons.
good_ending.title: User Rights Over Statistics
good_ending.learning: Success against diluter managers requires focusing on user rights and values rather than engaging with statistical minimization. Privacy protection shouldn't depend on complaint volumes or industry benchmarks.
